title: Kerala (Kochi, Munnar, Alappuzha)
selection: Kerala recorded 0.738 million foreign tourist visits in 2024 (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025, Table 4.1.2), up 13.8% on 2023, and is India's best-known backwater and hill-station destination. Kochi is the main international gateway; Munnar and Alappuzha are the most-visited hill and backwater bases.

places.name: Kerala
places.summary: Backwaters and houseboats, tea hills at Munnar, Kochi's spice-trade history and some of India's best food.
places.seoTitle: Kerala Travel Guide: Kochi, Munnar, Alappuzha & Backwaters
places.seoDescription: Plan a Kerala trip: Kochi's Fort and Mattancherry, Munnar's tea hills and Eravikulam, Alappuzha's backwaters and houseboats, food, festivals and the best season.

images.commons: File:Kerala backwaters, Canal, Palm trees, India.jpg
images.alt: A quiet backwater canal in Kerala lined with coconut palms and a moored canoe
images.caption: Kerala backwaters

overview.text:
Kerala, on India's south-west coast, is known for its backwaters — a web of lakes, canals and rivers that runs along nearly half the length of the state — and for the green hills of the Western Ghats behind them. It recorded 22.25 million domestic and 0.738 million foreign tourist visits in 2024.

The classic first trip links three places. Kochi, the old spice port, is the gateway, with its Chinese fishing nets, colonial churches and the synagogue and palace of Mattancherry. Munnar, about 1,600 m up in the Ghats, is tea country, with Eravikulam National Park and its Nilgiri tahr next door. Alappuzha is the base for a night on a houseboat in the backwaters.

Kerala's culture is as much a draw as its landscapes: Kathakali dance-drama, the martial art Kalaripayattu, the sadya feast on a banana leaf, and Onam, the harvest festival, in August–September.

items.body: Allow at least five days to combine Kochi, Munnar and the backwaters without rushing.
Book houseboats and Munnar hotels early for the October–February peak and Onam.
Expect heavy rain in the monsoon — beautiful, but roads to the hills can be slow.

places.name: Kochi
places.summary: Kerala's historic spice port and gateway: Chinese fishing nets, colonial Fort Kochi, Mattancherry's palace and synagogue, Kathakali and seafood.
places.seoTitle: Kochi Travel Guide: Fort Kochi, Mattancherry & Backwaters
places.seoDescription: Plan your Kochi trip: Fort Kochi's fishing nets and churches, Mattancherry Palace and the synagogue, Kathakali, food, the water metro and getting to Munnar.

images.alt: Chinese fishing nets on wooden frames along the shore at Fort Kochi
images.caption: Chinese fishing nets, Fort Kochi

overview.text:
Kochi has been a port since at least the 14th century, when ships from across Asia and Europe came for its spices; it is still called the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'. The Portuguese arrived in 1500, the Dutch in 1663 and the British in the 18th century, and each left its mark.

The city is spread out. Fort Kochi and Mattancherry, on the peninsula, hold the history: Chinese fishing nets on the shore, St Francis Church, colonial streets full of galleries, and the palace and synagogue of Mattancherry. Ernakulam, across the water, is the modern city with the stations and hotels. India's first water metro links the mainland with the islands.

Kochi is the usual gateway to Munnar and the backwaters, and October to March is the most pleasant time to visit.

items.body: The Chinese fishing nets at sunset in Fort Kochi.
St Francis Church, one of India's oldest European churches.
Mattancherry Palace's murals and the Paradesi Synagogue.
A Kathakali performance at the Kerala Kathakali Center.
The Kochi-Muziris Biennale of contemporary art, when it's on.

best_time.text: October to March has the most pleasant weather for exploring Kochi. December is busy: the ten-day Cochin Carnival takes over Fort Kochi, and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale of contemporary art runs over the winter in Biennale years.

how_to_reach.text: Cochin International Airport — the world's first fully solar-powered airport — serves Kochi with domestic and international flights. Ernakulam Junction is the main railway station; book on IRCTC. From Kochi, Munnar and Alappuzha are both easy road trips.

local_transport.text: Fort Kochi and Mattancherry are best explored on foot or by bicycle. To cross between Ernakulam and the islands, use the ferries or the Kochi Water Metro, India's first. Taxis and auto-rickshaws cover the rest.

where_to_stay.text: Fort Kochi, with its heritage homestays and small hotels, puts you among the sights and the cafes. Ernakulam on the mainland is more convenient for the station and has more large hotels, but you'll need a ferry or taxi to reach the old town.

items.body: Puttu with kadala (black chickpea) curry for breakfast.
Fish molee — fish in a mild coconut gravy.
A sadya, the vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf.
Fresh seafood from the stalls beside the fishing nets.

items.title: How many days do I need in Kochi?
items.body: One to two days for Fort Kochi and Mattancherry, plus an evening for Kathakali.

items.title: When is the synagogue open?
items.body: It is closed on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and Jewish holidays — plan around these days.

items.title: How far is Munnar from Kochi?
items.body: Munnar is about 119 km from Cochin International Airport.

places.name: Fort Kochi
places.summary: The old colonial quarter of Kochi: Chinese fishing nets, St Francis Church, Santa Cruz Basilica and streets of galleries and cafes.
places.seoTitle: Fort Kochi Guide: Chinese Fishing Nets & St Francis Church
places.seoDescription: Explore Fort Kochi: the Chinese fishing nets at sunset, St Francis Church where Vasco da Gama was buried, Santa Cruz Basilica, Kathakali and art galleries.

images.commons: File:Sunset with Chinese Fishing Nets, Fort Kochi 2.jpg
images.alt: Silhouettes of Chinese fishing nets against the sunset sky at Fort Kochi
images.caption: Fishing nets at sunset

overview.text:
Fort Kochi is the old heart of Kochi, shaped by Portuguese, Dutch and British rule. Its symbol is the row of Chinese fishing nets on the shore — huge cantilevered nets believed to have been introduced by Chinese traders. Watch them being raised in the late afternoon, then stay for sunset.

Behind the shore lie colonial streets full of art galleries and cafes. St Francis Church, first built in 1503, is one of the oldest European churches in India; Vasco da Gama died in Kochi in 1524 and was first buried here, before his remains were moved to Lisbon. The Santa Cruz Basilica nearby is known for its stained glass and painted interior. In the evening, catch a Kathakali performance at the Kerala Kathakali Center.

items.body: Walk or hire a bicycle — the area is compact.
Go to the fishing nets late in the afternoon for the catch and the sunset.
Book Kathakali tickets for the evening performance.

places.name: Mattancherry
places.summary: Kochi's old spice-trade quarter: the Dutch Palace with its murals, the 1568 Paradesi Synagogue and the antique shops of Jew Town.
places.seoTitle: Mattancherry, Kochi: Dutch Palace, Synagogue & Jew Town
places.seoDescription: Visit Mattancherry in Kochi: Mattancherry (Dutch) Palace and its Kerala murals, the Paradesi Synagogue of 1568, Jew Town's antique shops and opening days.

images.alt: The yellow-walled, tile-roofed Mattancherry Palace in Kochi
images.caption: Mattancherry (Dutch) Palace

overview.text:
Mattancherry, just east of Fort Kochi, was once a busy centre of the spice trade, and many communities — Jews, Konkanis, Gujaratis and others — settled here. Its two great sights are side by side.

Mattancherry Palace, popularly called the Dutch Palace, holds fine Kerala murals of Hindu religious scenes along with portraits and possessions of the Rajas of Kochi. Next door, the Paradesi Synagogue was built in 1568 for the city's Paradesi Jewish community; it is closed on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and Jewish holidays. The lanes of Jew Town around it are lined with antique and spice shops.

items.title: Paradesi Synagogue
items.body: Closed on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and Jewish holidays.

items.title: Mattancherry Palace
items.body: Check current opening days and fees before you go.
Visit on a weekday from Monday to Thursday to see both the palace and the synagogue.
Combine with Fort Kochi — it's a short walk or auto-rickshaw ride.

places.name: Munnar
places.summary: Kerala's tea-country hill station at about 1,600 m: rolling estates, lakes, Eravikulam National Park and the twelve-yearly Neelakurinji bloom.
places.seoTitle: Munnar Travel Guide: Tea Estates, Eravikulam & Best Time
places.seoDescription: Plan a Munnar trip: tea estates and the Tata Tea Museum, Eravikulam National Park, lakes and viewpoints, how to get there from Kochi and when to go.

images.alt: Terraced tea plantations covering the hills above Munnar town
images.caption: Tea plantations above Munnar

images.alt: Panorama of green tea estates and distant mountains near Munnar
images.caption: Tea country around Munnar

overview.text:
Munnar — the name means 'three rivers' — sits where three mountain streams meet, about 1,600 m up in the Western Ghats. In the colonial era it was a summer retreat, and from the late 19th century its slopes were planted with tea; today the estates roll away in every direction.

The Tata Tea Museum at Nallathanni Estate tells the plantation story and ends with a tasting. Beyond the tea, Munnar has lakes such as Mattupetty and Kundala for boating, and Eravikulam National Park, home of the Nilgiri tahr, just outside town. Anamudi, the highest peak in South India at 2,695 m, rises nearby. Every twelve years the hills turn blue when the Neelakurinji shrub flowers.

Munnar is about 119 km from Cochin International Airport.

best_time.text: December to February is cool and pleasant. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain — lush, but with mist and slow mountain roads.

how_to_reach.text: The nearest airport is Cochin International, about 119 km away, and the nearest railhead is Ernakulam Junction, about 120 km. From there, the drive up into the hills takes several hours; buses run from most major towns in Kerala.

items.body: Visit the Tata Tea Museum and its tasting room.
Take the shuttle into Eravikulam National Park to see the Nilgiri tahr.
Go boating on Mattupetty or Kundala lake.
Walk through the tea estates in the early morning mist.
Bring a warm layer — evenings are cool.
Start early: mist often rolls in during the afternoon.
Hill roads are slow; don't plan a same-day return to Kochi.

places.name: Eravikulam National Park
places.summary: Kerala's first national park, above Munnar, home to the largest population of the endangered Nilgiri tahr.
places.seoTitle: Eravikulam National Park: Nilgiri Tahr, Timings & Tips
places.seoDescription: Visit Eravikulam National Park near Munnar: the Nilgiri tahr, the Rajamala tourism zone, shuttle-only entry, opening hours and the Neelakurinji bloom.

images.alt: A young Nilgiri tahr, a mountain goat, grazing on grass
images.caption: The Nilgiri tahr, the species Eravikulam protects

overview.text:
Eravikulam, established in 1978, was Kerala's first national park. It was created to protect the endangered Nilgiri tahr, a mountain goat, and today shelters the largest population of the species. Lion-tailed macaques and Nilgiri langurs also live here.

Most of the park is closed to the public; visitors can only enter the tourism zone at Rajamala, on the road from Munnar. Private vehicles aren't allowed inside, so you continue by the park's own transport and on foot. The views take in Anamudi, South India's highest peak, and once every twelve years the slopes turn blue with Neelakurinji flowers.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 7 am – 6 pm (Ministry of Tourism listing). The park may close for part of the year — check before you go.

items.title: Access
items.body: Tourism zone at Rajamala only; no private vehicles inside.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check current fees with Kerala's Forest Department before visiting.

places.name: Alappuzha (Alleppey)
places.summary: The backwater capital of Kerala: houseboats on lakes and canals, the Nehru Trophy snake-boat race, beaches and Ayurveda.
places.seoTitle: Alappuzha Guide: Backwaters, Houseboats & Boat Race
places.seoDescription: Plan an Alappuzha (Alleppey) trip: houseboat cruises on the backwaters, the Nehru Trophy Boat Race, the beach, local food, Ayurveda and the best time to go.

images.alt: A traditional Kerala houseboat with a curved woven roof on the backwaters near Alappuzha
images.caption: Houseboat on the backwaters

overview.text:
Alappuzha — Alleppey — sits about 62 km south of Kochi and is the gateway to Kerala's most famous backwaters. Lord Curzon called it the 'Venice of the East'. The waterways here link five lakes and 38 rivers, threading past paddy fields, villages and coconut palms.

The classic way to see them is from a houseboat. These wooden boats once carried rice and spices; now they are floating rooms with bedrooms, bathrooms and a deck, and an overnight cruise is one of Kerala's defining experiences. On land, Alappuzha has a beach with a pier over 137 years old and a lighthouse, Ayurvedic centres, and the Ambalappuzha Sri Krishna Temple, famous for its sweet palpayasam. On the second Saturday of August, the Nehru Trophy Boat Race brings snake boats with crews of rowers to Punnamada Lake.

best_time.text: October to February is the ideal time to visit Alappuzha. Come in August for the Nehru Trophy Boat Race, held on the second Saturday of the month.

items.body: Karimeen pollichathu — pearl-spot fish cooked in banana leaf.
Puttu, vada and chickpea curry on a banana leaf.
Banana chips and pala appam.
Book houseboats through operators approved by Kerala Tourism, and confirm what's included (meals, route, cruising hours).
An overnight houseboat stay is the classic experience; a day cruise is the budget alternative.
Book well ahead for the Nehru Trophy race and the October–February peak.
